title: Mang Ernesto’s go-bag
note: Fictional unit and patients. DRAFT pending clinical sign-off. Your unit protocol, the attending nephrologist and your local disaster authorities decide every real event.
intro: Mr. Ernesto Villanueva, 67, on hemodialysis through a left forearm fistula, and his daughter Liza bring his go-bag to the pre-season check. It holds a two-year-old prescription photocopy, loose mixed pills, instant noodles, two bananas, a phone with no power bank and a note with the unit’s landline.

n1.prompt: What do you do about his emergency card?

choices.text: Fill in a new card: access type and side, dry weight, last potassium with its date, medicines, allergies, PhilHealth number, this unit and the backup unit with two phone numbers, and a family contact. Liza photographs it.
choices.feedback: A receiving unit needs exactly these facts to dialyze him safely.

choices.text: Write his name and the unit’s phone number on a card for now.
choices.feedback: Better than nothing, but a strange unit would still have to guess his access, dry weight and medicines.
choices.then: You complete the full card before he leaves.

choices.text: Keep the old prescription photocopy; it has most of the facts.
choices.feedback: It is two years old. His dry weight and medicines have changed.
choices.then: Liza asks for a proper card, and you make one.

n2.prompt: What do you say about the noodles and bananas?

choices.text: Swap them: noodles and their seasoning are very salty and bananas are high in potassium. Choose white rice, unsalted crackers and drained canned fruit, use one measured cup for drinks, give him the three-day diet sheet, and fill in his fluid allowance with him.
choices.feedback: The emergency diet limits potassium, salt and fluid until the next session; the sheet gives the amounts and the team sets his fluid number.

vitals.note: Diet sheet given; fluid allowance filled in

choices.text: Keep the bananas: they help with cramps.
choices.feedback: Bananas are high in potassium, which builds up dangerously between missed sessions.
choices.then: The dietitian, passing by, explains the risk and goes through the three-day diet sheet with them.

vitals.note: Diet sheet given; fluid allowance filled in

choices.text: The noodles are fine if he drinks less water with them.
choices.feedback: The salt drives thirst; limiting fluid after salty food is very hard.
choices.then: You give him the three-day diet sheet and fill in his fluid allowance.

vitals.note: Diet sheet given; fluid allowance filled in

n3.scene: Liza asks: “If the power goes out while he is on the machine, should he pull the needles out himself? Patients abroad are taught to.”

choices.text: No. Here, patients stay calm, stay connected, keep the fistula arm still and wait; a nurse comes to take him off safely. Pulling needles under stress can cause bleeding and lose the fistula.
choices.feedback: That is the Academy rule. In a six-country study, fewer than half of patients identified even the first stage of self-disconnection correctly.

choices.text: Show her how to pull the needles and press on the sites, just in case.
choices.feedback: Self-disconnection is not taught; it risks bleeding, air entry and a lost access.
choices.then: The charge nurse corrects this and teaches the rule instead.

choices.text: Tell her to ask the nephrologist at the next visit.
choices.feedback: The rule is already clear; give it now and explain why.
choices.then: You explain the rule before they leave.

end.title: Ready
end.text: Mang Ernesto leaves with a current card, a written medicine list and an agreed extra supply, the three-day diet sheet with his fluid allowance filled in, a power bank on Liza’s list, and one rule he can say back: stay calm, stay connected, protect the arm, wait for staff.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • The card carries what a stranger needs: access, dry weight, last potassium, medicines, allergies, units and contacts.
  • The emergency diet limits potassium, salt and fluid; the sheet gives the amounts and the team sets the fluid number.
  • Patients are not taught to self-disconnect. They stay connected and wait for staff.
